title_en: Hainan Province Yangpu Economic Development Zone Primary People's Procuratorate v. Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling — case of smuggling precursor chemicals
ruling_gist_en: 1. Whether an item constitutes a precursor chemical shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of relevant national laws and administrative regulations. Where relevant national laws and administrative regulations do not classify an item as a precursor chemical, even if such item can be used to manufacture drugs, it shall not be recognized as a precursor chemical.
keywords_en: Criminal; Smuggling precursor chemicals; First instance; Basic People's Court; Hainan Province; Natural person; Criminal Law; Whether hydrochloric acid constitutes a precursor chemical; Whether there is criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals; Smuggling hydrochloric acid; Identification of precursor chemicals; Legitimate production and operation; Smuggling; Drugs
full_text_en:
Yangpu Economic Development Zone Primary People's Procuratorate, Hainan Province v. Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling — smuggling of drug-making substances

[Ruling Summary]

1. Whether a substance is a drug-making substance shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of relevant national laws and administrative regulations. If the relevant national laws and administrative regulations do not stipulate it as a drug-making substance, even if the substance can be used to manufacture drugs, it cannot be identified as a drug-making substance.

2. According to Article 350 of the Criminal Law, the crime of smuggling drug-making substances requires the perpetrator to have the criminal intent of knowingly smuggling such substances. If the perpetrator truly does not know that the smuggled substances are drug-making substances, and the purpose of the smuggling is for legitimate production and operation, then even if the substances can be used for drug manufacturing, the perpetrator cannot be found to have the criminal intent of smuggling drug-making substances.

Procuratorial Authority: Yangpu Economic Development Zone Primary People's Procuratorate, Hainan Province

Defendant: Xie Jiewei (formerly known as Xie Guohua), male, 49 years old, Han Chinese, businessman. Arrested on September 11, 2002 in connection with this case.

Defendant: Liang Yanling, female, 47 years old, Han Chinese, housewife, wife of Xie Jiewei. Criminally detained on August 3, 2002 in connection with this case, and arrested on September 11 of the same year.

On September 25, 2003, the Yangpu Economic Development Zone Primary People's Procuratorate, Hainan Province, filed a public prosecution with the Yangpu Economic Development Zone People's Court, Hainan Province, against the defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling on charges of smuggling drug-making substances.

The indictment alleged:

In late December 2001, defendant Xie Jiewei established Vietnam Hai Huang Liability Company Limited (hereinafter referred to as Hai Huang Company) in Vietnam, engaging in the processing and production of shrimp shell meal and shrimp shell extract. Because the production required a large quantity of hydrochloric acid, Xie Jiewei discussed with Huang Yaoyuan, the security manager of Macau Tourism and Entertainment Co., Ltd., about purchasing a ship to transport hydrochloric acid and caustic soda from China to Vietnam, and then transporting shrimp shell meal back to China for sale. Huang Yaoyuan immediately agreed to invest. Xie Jiewei and Huang Yaoyuan respectively entrusted Hou Qing and Huang Yaoming (Huang Yaoyuan's younger brother) to set up the Hai Huang Company office in Haikou City, Hainan Province, responsible for the sales of shrimp shell meal.

On January 8, 2002, Xie Jiewei leased a motor vessel named "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" from Zhu Yuanyan at an annual rent of RMB 22,000, intending to use the vessel to transport hydrochloric acid and caustic soda to Vietnam, and then transport shrimp shell meal back to China for sale. In March 2002, Xie Jiewei obtained approval from Vietnam to import 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid.

Thereafter, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, in three batches on May 5, 2002, June 28, 2002, and July 13, 2002, respectively purchased 55.76 tons (payment: RMB 8,101.88), 52.12 tons (payment: RMB 7,572.99), and 52.3 tons (payment: RMB 7,599.15) of hydrochloric acid from within China. Without going through any lawful export procedures, they organized and directed others to smuggle the said hydrochloric acid to Vietnam. Among these, the first batch of hydrochloric acid was shipped to Vietnam, while the second and third batches were seized by the public security authorities during the smuggling process.

The prosecutorial authority argued:

The defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, without going through lawful exit procedures, illegally smuggled the precursor chemical hydrochloric acid in large quantities. Their conduct has violated the provisions of Article 350 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Criminal Law) and constitutes the crime of smuggling drug-making substances. Both defendants played major roles in the joint crime and are the principal offenders in this case. We request that they be punished according to law.

Defendant Xie Jiewei argued:

In November 2001, in accordance with international investment law and with the approval of the government of the host country, I registered and established Hai Huang Company in the Xi You Industrial Development Zone of Khanh Hoa Province, Vietnam. The main business scope is to purchase local discarded shrimp shells and crab shells, wash them with hydrochloric acid and caustic soda, and process them into shrimp shell extract or shell powder for local sale or export. Since there are very few manufacturers of hydrochloric acid in Vietnam, supply falls short of demand, and the price is very high. To facilitate production, reduce product costs, and solve the problems of insufficient local supply of hydrochloric acid and caustic soda raw materials and product export, Hai Huang Company applied to the relevant government departments of Vietnam for importing hydrochloric acid and caustic soda raw materials, and has obtained approval for importing 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid. The hydrochloric acid purchased by Hai Huang Company is mainly used for soaking and washing shrimp shells and crab shells.

Thereafter, Hai Huang Company commissioned Guangdong Maoming Maodong Large-Scale Automobile Transportation Co., Ltd. to purchase hydrochloric acid from Guangxi Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd., and to handle the procedures for export to Vietnam and the specific transportation matters. After Guangdong Maoming Maodong Large-Scale Automobile Transportation Co., Ltd. contacted the hydrochloric acid supplier, because Hai Huang Company had doubts about the coordination between the customs and joint inspection departments of the Vietnamese government, it decided to first import a small batch of hydrochloric acid from China without going through the relevant procedures, operating on a trial basis. After coordinating various relations later, it would import large quantities from China, which would also allow it to enjoy preferential policies such as export tax rebates in China.

Based on the above considerations, in May 2002, we purchased two batches of hydrochloric acid from Guangxi Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd., totaling 55.17 tons and 52.16 tons, at a price of RMB 220 per ton. For the first batch of 55.17 tons of hydrochloric acid, no export procedures were handled, no customs declaration was made, and no customs duties were paid, but the import procedures were handled in accordance with normal international trade practices. After the goods arrived in Vietnam, Hai Huang Company received the goods smoothly and used that batch for shrimp shell extract production. For the second batch of 52.16 tons of hydrochloric acid, it was still transported from Guangxi to Vietnam using the same method. When passing through Yangpu, Hainan, the ship encountered some minor malfunctions, and at the same time, the Vietnamese shipping agency did not handle the entry procedures for Hai Huang Company. Therefore, the ship carrying the batch docked at Yangpu Port, simultaneously repairing the ship and waiting for the entry procedures to be handled by the Vietnamese side. During this period, the ship was seized by the Yangpu Ganchong Border Police Station.

It is a fact that Hai Huang Company has set up a factory in Vietnam to process shrimp shells and crab shells. This production indeed requires the use of hydrochloric acid, and Hai Huang Company's purchase of hydrochloric acid is entirely for production needs. There are many manufacturers of hydrochloric acid in China with large production quantities, the market is oversupplied, the price is low, and it is permitted to trade freely in the domestic market and should also be allowed for export. The Criminal Law of China does not stipulate that buying, selling, or transporting hydrochloric acid constitutes a crime. Hai Huang Company's import of hydrochloric acid has been approved by the Vietnamese government. The reason for not declaring customs in China is mainly due to doubts about the coordination of relevant Vietnamese departments and worry that poor coordination might affect production. This approach was wrong, and I am willing to accept administrative or economic penalties. However, I truly did not know that hydrochloric acid is a drug-making substance, and I should not be convicted and punished for the crime of smuggling drug-making substances.

Defense counsel for defendant Xie Jiewei raised no objection to the fact alleged by the prosecutorial authority that Xie Jiewei purchased 55.76 tons of hydrochloric acid from Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd. in May 2002 and transported it to Vietnam. However, counsel argued that in June 2002, when Xie Jiewei again purchased 52.12 tons of hydrochloric acid from Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd., it was seized while docked at Yangpu Port, Hainan, and therefore this smuggling act should be considered as an attempt; on July 13, 2002, when Xie Jiewei purchased 52.3 tons of hydrochloric acid from Zhaoqing Chengde Chemical Co., Ltd. in Guangdong, this batch of hydrochloric acid was still undergoing customs approval procedures after being loaded onto the ship and was seized before departure, and therefore this act should not be treated as smuggling.

Counsel argued that based on the facts of this case, Xie Jiewei's conduct does not constitute a crime. First, Xie Jiewei's smuggling of hydrochloric acid lacks social harm. Xie Jiewei invested in and established Hai Huang Company in Vietnam, engaged in the production of shrimp shell meal and shrimp shell extract, which indeed requires large quantities of hydrochloric acid in the production process. Because the price of hydrochloric acid differs significantly between China and Vietnam, and to reduce production costs, hydrochloric acid was imported from China. The products of Hai Huang Company are not drugs, and smuggling hydrochloric acid has nothing to do with drug manufacturing. China's export tariff on hydrochloric acid is zero, and if customs declaration had been made normally, it could also enjoy preferential policies such as export tax rebates. Therefore, Xie Jiewei's conduct caused no loss to customs revenue. On the contrary, the Vietnamese government approved Hai Huang Company to import 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid from China in March 2002, which could increase China's foreign trade export volume, benefit the production and operation of Chinese enterprises and worker employment, and bring significant economic and social benefits. Of course, violating customs supervision regulations by smuggling hydrochloric acid is not to be advocated or supported, but Xie Jiewei's conduct should not be treated as a crime. Second, Xie Jiewei's smuggling of hydrochloric acid does not have criminal illegality. The Criminal Law, the Decision on Drug Control promulgated by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, and the relevant judicial interpretations of the Supreme People's Court do not stipulate that hydrochloric acid is a drug-making substance. Although the appendix to the Regulations on the Administration of Import and Export of Precursor Chemicals, promulgated in 1999 by the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation to fulfill obligations under the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances of 1988, listed hydrochloric acid, the Notice on Strengthening the Management of Production and Operation of Precursor Chemicals, jointly issued on November 21, 2000 by the State Economic and Trade Commission, the Ministry of Public Security, and the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, did not include hydrochloric acid as a precursor chemical in its appendix. Furthermore, the Regulations on the International Verification Administration of Import and Export of Precursor Chemicals (Wai Jing Mao Mao Fa [2002] No. 147), issued on June 1, 2002 by the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation and the Ministry of Public Security, also formulated to fulfill the obligations under the 1988 Convention, did not list hydrochloric acid as a precursor chemical. At the same time, Chinese customs also regulates hydrochloric acid as an ordinary commodity. Where Chinese law has clear provisions, international conventions cannot be directly applied. Therefore, according to the provisions of China's current laws and regulations, hydrochloric acid cannot be determined as a drug-making substance. In addition, even if hydrochloric acid were a drug-making substance, Xie Jiewei cannot be found to have the criminal intent of smuggling drug-making substances. Xie Jiewei did not know whether hydrochloric acid was a drug-making substance; what he purchased was all by-product hydrochloric acid with a concentration below 30%, which is a civilian chemical. The purpose of Xie Jiewei's smuggling of hydrochloric acid was to meet the needs of processing and producing shrimp shell meal and shrimp shell extract at the Hai Huang Company he established. The products produced have no connection with drugs, and Hai Huang Company's production requires dozens of tons of hydrochloric acid daily, so the hydrochloric acid Xie Jiewei purchased could not have been used for drug manufacturing. His motive for smuggling was to save money and trouble; if he had made a normal customs declaration, his conduct would not have been obstructed. Based on this, Xie Jiewei's smuggling of hydrochloric acid cannot be found to constitute the crime of smuggling drug-making substances. At the same time, because the value of the smuggled hydrochloric acid that can be determined is only approximately RMB 15,000, and China's export tariff on hydrochloric acid is zero, his smuggling of hydrochloric acid also does not constitute the crime of smuggling ordinary goods. In summary, although Xie Jiewei's conduct of smuggling hydrochloric acid violates customs supervision regulations, it should not be treated as a crime.

Defendant Liang Yanling argued: Defendant Xie Jiewei established Hai Huang Company in Vietnam which requires large quantities of hydrochloric acid as raw material. Hai Huang Company is engaged in the production of shrimp shell extract, not drug manufacturing. Moreover, the hydrochloric acid Hai Huang Company purchased is all low-concentration by-product hydrochloric acid. I did not know that hydrochloric acid can be used to manufacture drugs, nor did I have the criminal purpose of smuggling drug-making substances. I am a housewife who only occasionally helped my husband Xie Jiewei with some auxiliary work such as making payments. I did not participate in the smuggling. I had no knowledge of the first batch of hydrochloric acid smuggling on May 5, 2002 as alleged in the indictment; although I paid for the second batch on June 28 of the same year, I did not participate in directing it and did not know whether the batch had lawful export documents; the third batch on July 13 of the same year was not ordered by me—rather, after the seller called, I telephoned Xie Jiewei, and Xie Jiewei said to accept the goods first and transport them after the procedures were completed.

Defense counsel for defendant Liang Yanling argued that the prosecutorial authority's charge of smuggling drug-making substances against Liang Yanling is not established. Liang Yanling is a housewife; it is normal for her to help her husband Xie Jiewei's Hai Huang Company by purchasing goods and paying part of the payment and wages. Hydrochloric acid is not a prohibited item in China, and the Criminal Law does not prohibit the sale of hydrochloric acid. The smuggled items in this case are low-concentration by-product hydrochloric acid, all of which were used for Hai Huang Company's production of shrimp shell meal and shrimp shell extract, not for drug manufacturing. Moreover, the company has already obtained approval from Vietnam to import 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid. In summary, Liang Yanling did not subjectively have the criminal intent of smuggling drug-making substances, and her conduct also lacks social harm and danger, and does not constitute a crime.

Facts Found by the Yangpu Economic Development Zone People's Court at First Instance:

In late November 2001, defendant Xie Jiewei established Vietnam Hai Huang Liability Company Limited (hereinafter referred to as Hai Huang Company) in Vietnam, engaging in the processing and production of shrimp shell meal and shrimp shell extract. Because the production required a large quantity of hydrochloric acid, Xie Jiewei discussed with Huang Yaoyuan, the security manager of Macau Tourism and Entertainment Co., Ltd., about purchasing a ship to transport hydrochloric acid and caustic soda from China to Vietnam, and then transporting shrimp shell meal back to China for sale. Huang Yaoyuan immediately agreed to invest. Xie Jiewei and Huang Yaoyuan respectively entrusted Hou Qing and Huang Yaoming (Huang Yaoyuan's younger brother) to set up the Hai Huang Company office in Haikou City, Hainan Province, responsible for the sales of shrimp shell meal.

On January 8, 2002, defendant Xie Jiewei leased a motor vessel named "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" from Zhu Yuanyan at an annual rent of RMB 22,000, intending to use the vessel to transport hydrochloric acid and caustic soda to Vietnam, and then transport shrimp shell meal back to China for sale. In March 2002, Xie Jiewei obtained approval from Vietnam to import 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid.

On May 5, 2002, through the introduction of Lin Dexing, a salesman of Guangdong Maoming Maodong Large-Scale Automobile Transportation Co., Ltd., defendant Xie Jiewei purchased 55.76 tons of hydrochloric acid (payment: RMB 8,101.88) from Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd. through Huang Yanxing, manager of Guangdong Xinhui Huicheng Guangzheng Materials Co., Ltd. Lin Dexing arranged for a tanker truck with license plate "Yue A04557" of Maoming Maodong Large-Scale Automobile Transportation Co., Ltd. to transport the batch of hydrochloric acid to Tieshan Port, Beihai, Guangxi. Without going through any lawful export procedures for this batch, Xie Jiewei organized and directed the loading of the hydrochloric acid onto the "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" vessel. Xie Jiewei handed over the "Huaxin 03" vessel nameplate and ship certificates to the captain Chen Guanying, and instructed Chen Guanying to use the "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" nameplate in China and the "Huaxin 03" nameplate in Vietnam. On May 12 of the same year, Chen Guanying directed Chen Mu and crew members Yang Weijin, Huang Weigui, and Li Yong to operate the "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" vessel carrying the hydrochloric acid to Nha Trang Port, Vietnam. En route, due to seeking shelter from wind, the vessel docked at Basuo Port, Hainan on May 14. Xie Jiewei instructed Hou Qing and Huang Yaoming to go to Basuo Port to provide the vessel with a replenishment of fuel and living expenses totaling RMB 6,800. On May 18, the vessel arrived at Nha Trang Port, Vietnam, and Xie Jiewei organized personnel to unload the batch of hydrochloric acid. On June 4 of the same year, the "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" vessel departed from Nha Trang Port and returned to Bohe Port, Dianbai County, Guangdong.

On June 28, 2002, defendant Xie Jiewei again contacted through Lin Dexing, and Huang Yanxing purchased 52.12 tons of hydrochloric acid (payment: RMB 7,572.99) from Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd. Lin Dexing arranged for a tanker truck with license plate "Yue K03885" of Maoming Maodong Large-Scale Automobile Transportation Co., Ltd. to transport the batch of hydrochloric acid to Tieshan Port, Beihai, Guangxi, and defendant Liang Yanling organized the loading of the batch onto the "Yue Zhanjiang 0002" vessel. Without going through any lawful export procedures, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling then instructed Chen Guanying, Chen Mu, and crew members Yang Weijin, Huang Weigui, Li Yong, and Yang Liu to transport the batch to Da Nang, Vietnam the following day. On June 30, due to seeking shelter from wind and ship mechanical failure, the vessel temporarily docked at Yangpu Port, Hainan. At approximately 10:00 a.m. on July 1, it was seized by officers of the Yangpu Border Police Station.

On July 13, 2002, defendant Xie Jiewei instructed defendant Liang Yanling to arrange through Lin Dexing for the purchase of 52.3 tons of hydrochloric acid (payment: RMB 7,599.15) from Zhaoqing Chengde Chemical Co., Ltd., Guangdong. Lin Dexing arranged for the tanker truck "Yue D03885" of Maoming Maodong Large-Scale Automobile Transportation Co., Ltd. to transport the batch to Tieshan Port, Beihai, Guangxi, and loaded the batch onto the "Hejiyun 386" vessel for transport to Vietnam. Because there were no lawful export procedures, the captain and crew refused to transport it. Later, it was seized by the public security authorities.

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence: relevant documentary materials of Hai Huang Company; certification materials from the Consular Department of the Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam; certification from Nanning Chemical Co., Ltd.; the ship lease agreement; special invoices for the purchase of hydrochloric acid; inspection reports on hydrochloric acid from Hainan Province Product Quality Supervision and Inspection Institute; inspection and quarantine certificates from the People's Republic of China; testimony of witnesses including Huang Yaoyuan, Huang Yaoming, Hou Qing, Chen Guanying, Chen Mu, Lin Dexing, Huang Weigui, Huang Jiafu, and Li Shulin; site photos; and photos of the items. The evidence is sufficient to confirm the above facts.

Issue in dispute in this case: Whether hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical substance, and whether the conduct of defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling constitutes the crime of smuggling drug-making substances.

Opinion of the Yangpu Economic Development Zone People's Court at First Instance:

According to Article 350 of the Criminal Law, the crime of smuggling drug-making substances refers to the act of illegally transporting, carrying, or mailing acetic anhydride, ether, chloroform, or other raw materials or ingredients used for manufacturing drugs across the national border (frontier) in violation of national regulations. The subject of this crime is a general subject; the object infringed is the state's import and export management order concerning acetic anhydride, ether, chloroform, or other special chemicals that can be used for drug manufacturing; the subjective element requires the criminal intent of smuggling drug-making substances, i.e., the perpetrator knowingly carries out the smuggling of special chemicals that are under state control and can be used for drug manufacturing; the objective element manifests as the perpetrator, in violation of national regulations, carrying out the act of illegally transporting, carrying, or mailing acetic anhydride, ether, chloroform, or other raw materials or ingredients used for manufacturing drugs across the national border (frontier). Looking at the facts of this case, the conduct of defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling does not constitute the crime of smuggling drug-making substances.

I. Under the current laws and regulations of China, hydrochloric acid cannot be determined as a precursor chemical substance.

Neither the Criminal Law, the Decision on Drug Control of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, nor the relevant judicial interpretations of the Supreme People's Court clearly stipulate that hydrochloric acid is a drug-making substance. To fulfill the obligations under the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances of 1988, the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation of China promulgated the Regulations on the Administration of Import and Export of Precursor Chemicals as Order No. 4 of 1999, which listed hydrochloric acid among the 22 types of precursor chemicals in its appendix. However, the Notice on Strengthening the Management of Production and Operation of Precursor Chemicals, jointly issued on November 21, 2000 by the State Economic and Trade Commission, the Ministry of Public Security, and the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, did not include hydrochloric acid in its appendix as a precursor chemical. Subsequently, the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation and the Ministry of Public Security further issued the Regulations on the International Verification Administration of Import and Export of Precursor Chemicals (Wai Jing Mao Mao Fa [2002] No. 147) in 2002, also formulated to fulfill the obligations under the 1988 Convention, which likewise did not list hydrochloric acid as a precursor chemical. Although there are contradictions among the above administrative regulations regarding whether hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical, in accordance with the principle that new regulations prevail over old ones, the new regulations shall prevail. In summary, China's current laws do not list hydrochloric acid as a precursor chemical, and the latest relevant administrative regulations and rules also do not stipulate that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical. Therefore, hydrochloric acid cannot be determined as a drug-making substance.

2. Based on the facts of this case, it cannot be determined that the defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling had the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals.

First, as discussed above, under the current laws and regulations of China, hydrochloric acid cannot be deemed a precursor chemical. Accordingly, the defendants' act of smuggling hydrochloric acid naturally did not constitute the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals.

Second, even if hydrochloric acid were a precursor chemical, the defendants' act of smuggling hydrochloric acid would not necessarily constitute the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals. According to the facts of this case, Xie Jiewei established Haihuang Company in Vietnam to engage in the production of shrimp shell extract and shrimp shell bran, which required the use of chemical raw materials such as hydrochloric acid and caustic soda. Because the local price of hydrochloric acid in Vietnam was higher than in China, in order to reduce production costs and increase business profits, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling purchased hydrochloric acid domestically and then smuggled it to Vietnam for use in production. Their conduct evinced an intent to smuggle and a purpose of illegal profit. However, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling were not aware whether hydrochloric acid constituted a precursor chemical, and the smuggled hydrochloric acid was by-product hydrochloric acid with a concentration below 30%. Their purpose in smuggling hydrochloric acid was for Haihuang Company to process and produce shrimp shell extract and shrimp shell bran, not to engage in illegal transactions in Vietnam, and certainly not to manufacture drugs. To this end, Haihuang Company, after filing an application, obtained an import approval from Vietnam for 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid. To establish the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals, there must be a subjective criminal intent of knowingly smuggling precursor chemicals. Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling clearly did not possess such criminal intent.

In summary, the basic facts alleged by the prosecutorial authority that the defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling smuggled hydrochloric acid are clear, but the charge that Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling committed the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals is not established. The defenses raised by Xie Jiewei, Liang Yanling, and their defense counsel that the defendants' conduct did not constitute the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals are sustainable and are hereby adopted.

Accordingly, the Yangpu Economic Development Zone People's Court, pursuant to Article 162, paragraph (2) of the Criminal Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Criminal Procedure Law), rendered the following judgment on August 13, 2004:

The defendants Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling are acquitted.

The Yangpu Economic Development Zone Primary People's Procuratorate, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, filed a protest with the Yangpu Economic Development Zone Intermediate People's Court. The main grounds for the protest were: 1. The facts found by the court of first instance were in part unclear. The defendant at first instance, Liang Yanling, participated in the smuggling of hydrochloric acid carried out on May 5, 2002, but the court of first instance did not find this fact. 2. The judgment of first instance erred in finding that the defendants at first instance, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, did not have the criminal intent of knowingly smuggling precursor chemicals. As long as the actor subjectively knew that he was smuggling hydrochloric acid, it can be determined that he had the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals. Whether the actor knew that hydrochloric acid was a precursor chemical cannot serve as a basis for determining whether he had the subjective intent to smuggle precursor chemicals. 3. The judgment of first instance applied the law incorrectly. The court of first instance erred in finding that the charge brought by the prosecutorial authority was not established on the ground that hydrochloric acid is not a precursor chemical under state control. The protesting authority requests that the court of second instance amend the judgment according to law and convict and sentence the two defendants at first instance for the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals.

The defendant at first instance, Xie Jiewei, argued in defense: I indeed did not know that hydrochloric acid was a precursor chemical. The judgment of first instance is correct, and I request that the court of second instance affirm the original judgment.

The defense counsel for the defendant at first instance, Xie Jiewei, argued: The court of first instance found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. The procuratorate's view in its protest that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical is not sustainable. Xie Jiewei's conduct does not satisfy the constituent elements of the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals. The defense counsel requests that the court of second instance reject the protest according to law and affirm the original judgment.

The defendant at first instance, Liang Yanling, argued in defense: I am merely a homemaker and had no idea whether hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical. The judgment of first instance found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. I request that the court of second instance reject the protest according to law and affirm the original judgment.

The defense counsel for the defendant at first instance, Liang Yanling, argued: First, administrative regulations may serve as a basis for administrative penalties but not as a basis for criminal punishment. Second, in domestic criminal trials, where national law has no express provision, international conventions cannot be directly invoked to convict and punish domestic citizens. Third, assuming the conduct of the defendant at first instance, Xie Jiewei, constituted the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals, only the smuggling of hydrochloric acid on the first two vessels could be punished as a crime. The hydrochloric acid on the third vessel was then docked at the port of Tieshan in Guangxi and was in a lawful state, and should not be punished as a crime. Fourth, assuming Xie Jiewei's conduct constituted a crime, Liang Yanling's conduct cannot be deemed a crime because there is no evidence that the two defendants shared a common criminal intent. Fifth, Liang Yanling did not know that hydrochloric acid was a precursor chemical, and therefore not only did she lack joint criminal intent, but she also lacked the subjective intent for an individual crime. In summary, Chinese law does not provide that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical. The provisions of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation cannot serve as the legal basis under criminal law for deeming hydrochloric acid a precursor chemical. Although hydrochloric acid can in fact be used to manufacture drugs, the conduct of the two defendants at first instance does not constitute the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals. The defense counsel requests that the court of second instance reject the protest and affirm the original judgment.

The Yangpu Economic Development Zone Intermediate People's Court, after trial on appeal, held that, based on the testimony of witnesses Chen Mu and Lin Zuoquan in this case and the confession of the defendant at first instance, Xie Jiewei, it could be found that the defendant at first instance, Liang Yanling, participated in the smuggling of hydrochloric acid carried out on May 5, 2002. The protest raised by the protesting authority on this ground is reasonable. The failure of the original judgment to find the above facts was improper and should be corrected. The court of second instance confirmed the other facts found by the original judgment.

The issues in dispute to be resolved in this appeal were: whether hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical, and whether the defendants at first instance, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, had the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals.

The Yangpu Economic Development Zone Intermediate People's Court held on appeal as follows:

First, under the relevant provisions of the current laws and administrative regulations of China, it cannot be determined that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical.

Pursuant to Article 350 of the Criminal Law, the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals refers to the act of illegally transporting, carrying, or sending acetic anhydride, ether, chloroform, or other raw materials or ingredients used for manufacturing drugs across the national (border) frontier in violation of state regulations. Accordingly, whether a certain substance constitutes a precursor chemical should be determined in accordance with relevant state regulations. Article 96 of the Criminal Law provides: "'Violation of state regulations' as used in this Law refers to violations of laws and decisions enacted by the National People's Congress and its Standing Committee, and administrative regulations, administrative measures, and orders and decisions promulgated by the State Council." Neither the Criminal Law of China, the Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Drug Prohibition, the relevant judicial interpretations of the Supreme People's Court, nor the relevant administrative regulations promulgated by the State Council expressly provide that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical. Although the appendix to the *Provisions on the Administration of Import and Export of Precursor Chemicals* promulgated by the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation by Decree No. 4 in 1999 listed hydrochloric acid among 22 types of precursor chemicals, that provision is a departmental regulation and cannot serve as a basis for criminal adjudication. Moreover, after that provision came into effect, the State Economic and Trade Commission, the Ministry of Public Security, and the State Administration for Industry and Commerce jointly issued the *Notice on Strengthening the Administration of Production and Operation of Precursor Chemicals* on November 21, 2000, and the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation and the Ministry of Public Security jointly issued the *Provisions on the Administration of International Verification of Import and Export of Precursor Chemicals* (WaiJingMaoFa [2002] No. 147) in 2002, neither of which listed hydrochloric acid as a precursor chemical. Under the principle that new provisions prevail over old ones, the new provisions should control; that is, even under the most recent departmental regulations, it cannot be determined that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical. In summary, it cannot be determined that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical, and accordingly, it cannot be determined that the conduct of the defendants at first instance, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, in smuggling hydrochloric acid constituted the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals.

Second, based on the facts of this case, even if hydrochloric acid could be used to manufacture drugs, it cannot be determined that the defendants at first instance, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, had the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals.

Upon investigation, it is true that the defendant at first instance, Xie Jiewei, established Haihuang Company in Vietnam to engage in the production of shrimp shell extract and shrimp shell bran, and it is also true that this production required the use of chemical raw materials such as hydrochloric acid and caustic soda. Because the local price of hydrochloric acid in Vietnam was higher than in China, in order to reduce production costs and increase business profits, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling purchased hydrochloric acid domestically and then smuggled it to Vietnam for use in production. Although their conduct evinced an intent to smuggle and a purpose of illegal profit, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling were not aware whether hydrochloric acid was a precursor chemical or whether it could be used to manufacture drugs, and the smuggled hydrochloric acid was by-product hydrochloric acid with a concentration below 30%. Their purpose in smuggling hydrochloric acid was for Haihuang Company to process and produce shrimp shell extract and shrimp shell bran, not to engage in illegal transactions in Vietnam, and certainly not to manufacture drugs. To this end, Haihuang Company, after filing an application, obtained an import approval from Vietnam for 22,000 tons of hydrochloric acid. According to the provisions of the Criminal Law, to establish the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals, there must be a subjective criminal intent of knowingly smuggling precursor chemicals. The ground for protest raised by the protesting authority—that "as long as the actor subjectively knew that he was smuggling hydrochloric acid, it can be determined that he had the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals, and whether the actor knew that hydrochloric acid is a precursor chemical cannot serve as a basis for determining whether he had the subjective intent to smuggle precursor chemicals"—cannot be sustained. In summary, it cannot be determined that Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling had the criminal intent to smuggle precursor chemicals.

In summary, although the original judgment was unclear with respect to some findings of fact, it correctly found that hydrochloric acid is not a precursor chemical under state control, that the defendants at first instance, Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling, did not have the criminal intent of knowingly smuggling precursor chemicals, and that their conduct in smuggling hydrochloric acid did not constitute the crime of smuggling precursor chemicals. The grounds for protest raised by the protesting authority cannot be sustained. Although Xie Jiewei and Liang Yanling carried out the act of smuggling hydrochloric acid, the value of the smuggled goods was only approximately RMB 15,000, and the evaded taxes amounted to less than RMB 50,000. Therefore, this conduct does not, according to law, constitute the crime of smuggling ordinary goods or articles.

Accordingly, the Yangpu Economic Development Zone Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 189, paragraph (1) of the Criminal Procedure Law, rendered the following ruling on February 17, 2005:

Reject the protest and affirm the original judgment.

This ruling is final.
